stories.headline: Update: Democrats Finalize Sweeping Midterm Wins as House Nominee Jeffries Draws 11 Dissenters and Oversight Chair Targets Trump Circle
stories.summary:
Democrats have completed a broad midterm victory, with Mary Peltola's win in Alaska securing a 56-44 Senate majority, according to the outlets covering the results. Aggregated coverage cites a 56% to 42% Democratic edge in the national House vote, described as the widest margin for either party in 50 years. Republican Rep. Nick Begich held Alaska's lone House seat after ranked-choice tabulation, one of few GOP bright spots. More than 30 House Republican incumbents lost their seats.

On Wednesday, House Democrats nominated Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries for speaker by a 251-11 tally in a closed-door caucus vote, which he requested be counted. He is on track to become the first Black speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3. The 11 dissenting members cited concerns including Medicare for All, immigration enforcement and Gaza, and some progressives criticized his record on corporate interests. Seven incoming members said publicly they had voted against him.

Incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia sent 12 document-preservation letters to Trump associates and relatives, including Vice President Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump and Jared Kushner, ahead of planned investigations into Trump family finances, DHS conduct and the handling of the Epstein files. Separately, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, issued a records-preservation notice to Rep. Jamie Raskin, accusing Democrats of planning to weaponize oversight. Sen. Elissa Slotkin called a separate Reitz inquiry into her remarks "baseless," citing the First Amendment and the Speech or Debate Clause, while Reitz says he is not interested in chilling speech.

Republicans are weighing their next steps after the losses, and House Republicans worry Democratic clout could trigger a shutdown fight before the Dec. 11 funding deadline. Democrats say the results are a rebuke of President Trump's agenda, while Republicans are split over the party's direction, and a Politico poll finds Americans broadly doubt the GOP's prospects.

stories.headline: JPMorgan Chase Says Customer Data Possibly Exposed in Attack on Third-Party Vendors
stories.summary:
JPMorgan Chase said Thursday morning that third-party vendors providing services to the bank were the target of a cyberattack, potentially exposing some customer information. The bank did not immediately detail how many customers were affected or what categories of data were involved.

The disclosure comes amid a week of heightened concern over technology failures in the United States, including outages that affected air traffic control and banking systems. Top homeland security and intelligence officials told Congress on Wednesday they had found no evidence of rogue AI agents or a foreign government behind those outages, attributing them to maintenance issues. Whether the JPMorgan incident is related to those events was not addressed in the available reporting.

Vendor-based breaches have become a common route into large financial institutions, since third parties often hold sensitive data while operating outside the bank's own security perimeter. Lawmakers from both parties have pressed the administration to do more to protect critical infrastructure from AI-aided cyberattacks. Further details on the scope of exposure and any customer notifications are expected as the bank's investigation continues.

stories.headline: Iowa Residents Told to Evacuate Before Army Detonates Five Tons of Lead Azide
stories.summary:
The Army is asking residents of Middletown, Iowa, to temporarily evacuate Friday ahead of a planned controlled detonation of 68 drums, about five tons, of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. The Army says the explosive chemical, used to set off munitions, has become an "explosive safety hazard" and was "deemed unsafe for relocation."

The EPA approved an emergency permit on Nov. 13, saying recrystallization of the material during long-term storage created a risk of spontaneous explosion due to its sensitivity to friction and shock. The agency determined the risk presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment. The Army says two rapid, consecutive detonations will cause a loud noise, ground vibrations and a dust plume containing some lead that should linger no more than an hour, depending on wind.

About 400 people live in Middletown, but thousands more lie in the path of the plume, and notifications went to communities up to 100 miles away. The Army first told residents of the need to dispose of the material in March after the plant paused operations for a review, and shared details at an October public meeting. Plant commander Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse said the safety of the plant's people and neighbors is non-negotiable.

stories.headline: Justice Department Sends Prosecutor Bill Essayli to Florida for Inquiry Into Mar-a-Lago Raid
stories.summary:
The Justice Department is sending Los Angeles federal prosecutor Bill Essayli to South Florida to work on a criminal investigation into the FBI's 2022 search of Mar-a-Lago and Jack Smith's handling of the classified documents case, according to multiple reports. A source confirmed to the Washington Examiner that Essayli's assignment is focused on the raid, and Politico reported it first.

Essayli is described as a staunch ally of President Trump. Supporters of the administration view the inquiry as accountability for what they regard as a politicized investigation of the president. Critics, including the Guardian, characterize it as pursuit of one of Trump's long-standing grievances and a further use of the Justice Department against his adversaries.

The move comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and plan oversight of the administration. It also follows other Justice Department actions this week, including letters from Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Texas, to Democratic lawmakers over their rhetoric. The scope and timeline of the Florida inquiry have not been disclosed.

stories.headline: El Niño-Fueled Storm Floods South Florida, Collapses Synagogue Roof; Emergency Declared
stories.summary:
A slow-moving storm system dumped heavy rain on South Florida on Wednesday, prompting an emergency declaration in Hollywood and leaving cars submerged along roads. Preliminary National Weather Service figures showed 15.3 inches (39 centimeters) of rain fell in a 24-hour period ending Wednesday in parts of Broward County. The highest amounts were recorded in Plantation.

Hollywood Mayor Josh Levy called it a "historically significant rainfall event" and urged motorists to stay off the roads. Portions of the Florida Turnpike and Interstate 95 in Hollywood were closed because of high water and stalled vehicles, and the city received more than 300 calls for service overnight. The roof of Temple Sinai in Hollywood collapsed, and a local hospital suffered roof damage and flooded hallways. No injuries were reported. Some residents said fast-moving drivers created wakes that pushed floodwater into their homes.

The Florida Division of Emergency Management warned of "potentially catastrophic" rainfall, flash flooding and life-threatening rip tides. The weather service said the threat should last through Friday along the Atlantic Coast, with up to 12 more inches possible. Meteorologist Alejandra Garcia said El Niño has disrupted the state's typical dry season by steering low-pressure systems toward the southeastern United States.

The storm comes ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, when travel is heavy. The National Hurricane Center said a low-pressure system expected to form near the northern Bahamas could become a subtropical or tropical storm over parts of the southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts into early next week. On the West Coast, heavy rain and wind grounded planes at San Francisco's airport, disrupted ferry service and flooded roads in Napa County.

stories.headline: Dozens Missing After Boat Carrying About 100 Migrants Sinks Off Senegal
stories.summary:
Senegalese authorities continued search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the country's coast. The badly damaged vessel washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Initial reports cited one death, but some local media said at least four bodies had been recovered, with dozens still missing.

A village chief's representative said the incident occurred around 02:00 local time, and that cries from the pirogue could be heard from the beach. A survivor told police there were about 100 people aboard, including five women. Police recovered identity documents, mobile phones and personal belongings, including a school enrolment document. Searches continued through Wednesday and were due to resume Thursday.

The disaster comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off Thieppe killed at least 39 people, one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters. President Diomaye Faye expressed concern at a cabinet meeting about a renewed increase in irregular departures and ordered the interior ministry to report on the causes and propose remedies.

The UN migration agency IOM has recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year, a figure it says is likely an underestimate. Tighter controls in North Africa have pushed migrants toward the Atlantic route to Spain's Canary Islands, where most arrivals this year are Senegalese. On Nov. 7, El Hierro declared a state of emergency after more than 3,300 people arrived in about 30 boats since the start of the month.

stories.headline: US-Led Consortium Wins $60 Billion Kenya Critical Minerals Tender, Beating Chinese Rivals
stories.summary:
A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven other bidders including companies from China and Australia. The site is estimated to hold critical mineral deposits worth more than $60 billion, including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defense technology. The consortium combines three US firms: Bunker Hill Mining, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies.

Frontier Minerals says its plan would keep more of the economic benefit in Kenya through in-country processing and refining. The deal fits Washington's push for greater access to African minerals to strengthen supply chains and reduce dependence on China, which dominates processing of several key minerals. The US has pursued similar partnerships with the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia.

The award faces hurdles. The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet regulatory requirements. Reuters reported that two rival companies plan to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging Frontier missed an earlier submission deadline. Kenya's government maintains the process was open and transparent.

The site, in Kwale County near the Indian Ocean coast, covers about 390 acres of forest. Local residents fear environmental damage and harm to ancestral heritage, and question whether nearby communities will benefit. Kenya's mining ministry says the sector is central to diversifying the economy beyond tourism, agriculture and financial services.

stories.headline: Update: Bots Amplified Conspiracy Theories and Panic Over Recent Tech Outages, Research Finds
stories.summary:
Bot accounts have helped spread conspiracy theories about a wave of major technology outages over the past week, according to new research shared exclusively with Axios. The outages and technology errors have piled up across multiple sectors, fueling public anxiety about fragile infrastructure.

The research indicates that purveyors of disinformation appear to be exploiting that anxiety, amplifying suspicions of coordinated cyberattacks and government cover-ups. It is unclear who is behind the accounts. The pattern suggests that when technology failures lack substantive explanations, false narratives can fill the vacuum.

The findings follow official statements that the outages were not part of a systemic attack. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said earlier that the US was not "under systemic attack," and officials attributed the recent outage of the NSA's classified internal network to software patching rather than a cyberattack.

stories.headline: Update: Trump, Xi and Putin Hold Unprecedented Three-Way Summit in Shenzhen
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met together on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It was the first time the leaders of the three nuclear powers have sat down as a trio. Trump also held a one-on-one meeting with Putin, their first in-person encounter in more than a year, and discussed Ukraine.

Russia said the three leaders agreed to boost oil and gas production and reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war. Trump said "we are really making history" and called for nuclear arms reduction. Putin noted that all three countries were victorious nations of World War II. Xi called his separate meeting with Trump "positive and constructive," signaling that a trade truce remains on track despite renewed tensions over US chip curbs.

The agenda also included Iran, trade, AI chips and the war in Ukraine. The last major US-Russia arms control treaty, New START, expired in February, and Trump wants China included in any new framework, which Beijing has resisted, arguing its arsenal is much smaller. Ukraine struck a key bridge to Crimea ahead of the summit, and Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were to meet Ukrainian and European officials in Berlin on security guarantees.

Reaction in Washington was divided. Some Republican lawmakers warned that Xi and Putin are "not our friends," while others defended a president willing to hold hard conversations with rival powers. Critics have questioned whether the meeting helps rehabilitate Putin on the world stage, while supporters see a chance for progress on arms control and ending the Ukraine war.

stories.headline: Update: Anthropic Raises Record $81 Billion in Stock Market Debut
stories.summary:
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, raised a record $81 billion in its initial public offering, with shares set to begin trading Thursday in New York. The stock priced at $83, above the proposed range of $70 to $78, after demand reportedly exceeded supply by more than ten times. BBC reports the pricing values the company at about $1.5 trillion.

The company will raise an additional $26 billion from share sales to technology firms including Nvidia. Underwriters could exercise a greenshoe option for another $12 billion, bringing the total to as much as $107 billion. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to sell shares publicly, and its seven founders become multibillionaires immediately.

The company's revenue reached $33 billion in the nine months to September, but net losses were $104 billion over the same period, according to its IPO filing. Analysts say the listing is a crucial test of investor appetite for AI, with questions persisting over when massive infrastructure spending will pay off. Canaccord Wealth's Leah Bramwell said demand was broad across institutional and retail investors rather than a retail-driven frenzy.

SpaceX raised $75 billion in its June listing and later saw its share price fall after an initial surge. OpenAI, Anthropic's chief rival, is expected to go public next year.

stories.headline: Update: Houthi Strikes Damage Saudi Public Investment Fund Headquarters in Riyadh
stories.summary:
The Riyadh skyscraper housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund was damaged, according to an eyewitness, after debris fell following the latest Houthi strikes launched toward Saudi Arabia. Material damage was reported at the King Abdullah Financial District, which includes the city's tallest building.

It was the second attack on the district this month, following a strike by the Iran-backed Houthis of Yemen on Nov. 8. The Public Investment Fund is the kingdom's sovereign wealth vehicle and a central player in its economic strategy.

The strikes come as the regional confrontation involving the United States, Israel and Iran continues. Iran recently attacked Bahrain and Kuwait following US strikes on Qeshm island, and the US and Iran remain locked in a standoff over the Strait of Hormuz. The attack widens the conflict's reach to Gulf financial infrastructure, though casualty figures and Saudi government responses were not immediately available.

stories.headline: Danish Parliament Approves Greenland Security Deal With US
stories.summary:
Denmark's parliament approved a trilateral agreement among the United States, Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The vote in the Folketing was 109-0, the final step before the deal enters into force. Greenland's parliament approved it earlier this month, also with no opposition.

The agreement paves the way for more US bases in Greenland while keeping the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.

The deal follows months of pressure from President Trump, who repeatedly called for the vast island to become part of the United States, straining relations with Denmark, a NATO ally. Supporters present the pact as a way to bolster Arctic defense and ease those tensions, while Danish and Greenlandic leaders have stressed that sovereignty remains with Copenhagen and Nuuk.
